audio_caption: The audio begins with a male speaker introducing a miniature lecture on solenoids, referring to previous discussions on magnetic fields from wires and loops. He then proceeds to explain that without going into too much detail about calculating magnetic fields, he hopes to motivate where the magnetic field for a solenoid comes from, why it looks the way that it does, and how one can use it in other problems.

The audio clip begins with a single male speaker explaining the concept of a solenoid, describing it as "a single loop of wire placed next to other single loops of wire." He goes on to characterize an ideal solenoid, describing the arrangement of the loops of wire. His tone is explanatory and straightforward.

The clip begins with one person explaining how to make a solenoid. He says to take a long piece of wire and curl it around a cylinder, creating turns of copper wire. He notes the importance of choosing the number of turns of copper wire. He continues, saying that a solenoid is a coil of wire tightly wound.

The clip features a male speaker discussing running an electric current through a solenoid and how the magnetic field of a single loop of conductor resembles a magnetic dipole field. He emphasizes that moving current is the primary source of magnetic fields, which leads to the dipole configuration. The speech is educational and explanatory. The speaker talks about why magnetic monopoles don't exist in nature and the need for complicated dipole fields.

One male speaker provides an explanation, beginning with the phrase "Now, imagine what would happen if...". He speaks in an instructional tone about loops of wire and magnetic fields. He mentions "little iron filings" and that the magnetic fields "are adding up". His tone is calm and measured. He states, "This is how you make a uniform magnetic field in practice". The recording ends abruptly.

A male speaker begins explaining the concept of a solenoid in a descriptive tone, mentioning the creation of "many windings of the wire," then how running a current through the wire results in "current circulating like water." He then details an ideal solenoid's behavior, describing it as producing an "extremely uniform magnetic field." The speaker continues, relating the principle to the creation of a strong uniform magnetic field in an MRI device. To illustrate, he references a computer map of the magnetic field inside an MRI solenoid, consisting of "many thousands of closely spaced windings of wire," leading to a very precise magnetic field especially at the central axis where the patient would be placed, noting its importance for the operation of the device.

The clip features a single male speaker explaining the magnetic field inside a solenoid. He presents a formula, breaking down each component, such as the permeability of free space, number of turns of wire ("that's the capital N"), current ("that's being driven through the wire"), and length of the solenoid. He sounds educational and clear, avoiding complex derivations and focusing on explanations. The speaker states the variables within the equation ("big N is the number of turns of wire"). He emphasizes that one can control the magnetic field by controlling the geometry of the solenoid.

The audio clip begins with a male speaker discussing the properties of a "tightly wound solenoid," stating that it can "give you a very strong magnetic field." He speaks in an informative, somewhat technical tone. He goes on to say you could weaken the magnetic field by increasing its length or reducing the number of turns of wire.

A single male speaker explains that when manufacturing a solenoid it's convenient to write n/l as a new number, writing it as a little n, which he says is referred to as the "number density". He further explains that this represents "the number of turns per unit length". He gives an example of buying a solenoid and how manufacturers will sell it as a certain density of turns per unit length. The speaker uses a tone that is calm and informative. He states, "this little n is a very convenient thing," which allows them to write the magnetic field as "mu naught times little n times I".

The audio clip begins with a male speaker concluding a lecture on "solenoidal magnetic field," mentioning the use of the solenoid as an "archetypal magnetic device" to discuss "magnetic induction." The speech has an educational and formal tone. No music or background sounds are present in the clip.
